articles.title: Piscante
articles.excerpt: Sem metáforas. Talvez essa seja uma palavra que é usada mais frequentemente caso você tenha um MacBook Pro M1 de 2020. Esse modelo tem versões com a famosa TouchBar. Que funcionou super bem durante um…
articles.body: Sem metáforas. Talvez essa seja uma palavra que é usada mais frequentemente caso você tenha um MacBook Pro M1 de 2020. Esse modelo tem versões com a famosa TouchBar. Que funcionou super bem durante um bom tempo por aqui. Só que faz alguns meses que a querida fica “piscando”. E aí tem algumas coisas que se pode fazer para tentar “arrumar”. Bom, importante dizer que quando tem iluminação suficiente, tudo certo, o problema não acontece. Quando fica em um ambiente com menos iluminação tipo sala de aula/palestra, ou quando estamos usando algum editor em “dark mode“, o problema começa. A TouchBar começa a piscar. O que eu já fiz por aqui. Desativei o “Ajustar automaticamente o brilho” na configuração das Telas. Aumento o brilho da tela ao máximo.

articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass Sagittarius is a local-first outdoor companion that runs as a single HTML file. You open it, check the sky, get…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Sagittarius is a local-first outdoor companion that runs as a single HTML file. You open it, check the sky, get a plan, and then close the laptop. Outing planner: pulls today's forecast (temperature, rain chance, wind, UV, sunrise and sunset) and suggests a plan for a hike, run, birding trip, foliage photo walk, gardening session or picnic, sized to the time you have. Field guide: a chat with an open-weight model running on your own machine. Describe a bird call, a plant or a trail question and get an answer, even with no signal. Garden planner: enter your frost dates (or pick a season if you have no frost) and see what to sow this week. It works fully offline.

articles.title: EcoSound: Using Open-Source AI to Get People Outside and Exploring Nature 🌿
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What if we used AI to get people off their screens instead of keeping them glued to them? That question inspired…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built What if we used AI to get people off their screens instead of keeping them glued to them? That question inspired me to build EcoSound, an open-source, AI-powered application that turns ordinary outdoor experiences into opportunities to discover wildlife. We're surrounded by nature, but how often do we actually stop to notice it? You might hear a bird singing outside your window, while walking through a park, or on your way to work, without knowing what it is. EcoSound makes those small moments of curiosity more meaningful.
articles.author: Daniel Chege

articles.title: AI Coding Agents Don’t Replace Developers — They Expose Skill Gaps
articles.excerpt: If you spend any time on developer forums these days, you’ll run into two loud takes. One camp swears AI coding agents will wipe out junior dev roles within years. The other side claims these tools ar…
articles.body: If you spend any time on developer forums these days, you’ll run into two loud takes. One camp swears AI coding agents will wipe out junior dev roles within years. The other side claims these tools are nothing more than fancy autocomplete, and human engineers will always remain in full control. After months of integrating agent workflows like Cursor into daily production work, I think both arguments miss the practical reality sitting right in our code editors. AI coding agents don’t remove coding work. They move the cognitive load. Pre-AI, most of my day was split: roughly 60% implementing logic, wiring up endpoints, writing boilerplate, debugging syntax and minor bugs; 40% system design, risk evaluation and requirement validation. With agent tools, that ratio flips completely.

articles.title: Tonkeeper Is Now Keeper: What the Multichain Shift Means for Wallet Architecture
articles.excerpt: Tonkeeper is no longer just a TON wallet. The product has been rebranded as Keeper and now supports seven networks: TON TRON Ethereum Bitcoin Arbitrum Base BNB Chain At first glance, this looks like a…
articles.body: Tonkeeper is no longer just a TON wallet. The product has been rebranded as Keeper and now supports seven networks: TON TRON Ethereum Bitcoin Arbitrum Base BNB Chain At first glance, this looks like a normal wallet expansion. Technically, however, moving from a single-chain wallet to a multichain product introduces a much harder problem: How do you make several incompatible blockchain systems feel like one wallet without hiding the differences that users still need to understand? Keeper’s rebrand is interesting because it shows both the benefits and the complexity of that transition. From a TON Wallet to a Multichain Interface Tonkeeper originally focused on TON.

articles.title: I Would Not Land the Edit Until the Server Tree Shared My Hash
articles.excerpt: I spent two days chasing a failing command, and the tempting shortcut was to let a model rewrite the file. Why would I keep hand-editing a small parser when a free model could draft the change? The tr…
articles.body: I spent two days chasing a failing command, and the tempting shortcut was to let a model rewrite the file. Why would I keep hand-editing a small parser when a free model could draft the change? The trouble started when the server copy and my laptop copy stopped being the same tree. Treat the notes below as a worked failure you can reproduce, not as a measured outage report. The failure I kept blaming on the edit The command was small, and that smallness made the miss much easier to excuse at first. I ran a Python check, watched it fail, and asked for a unified diff instead of a full rewrite. The diff looked tidy, applied on my laptop, and still failed after I copied those names into a clean directory.

articles.title: CI Email Tests Need a Run Manifest
articles.excerpt: Email assertions are often the least explainable part of an otherwise tidy CI pipeline. A browser test can tell you that a verification link was not found, but that sentence leaves out the useful deta…
articles.body: Email assertions are often the least explainable part of an otherwise tidy CI pipeline. A browser test can tell you that a verification link was not found, but that sentence leaves out the useful details: which inbox did the run own, when did the signup happen, and which messages were considered? I have started treating each email test like a small deployment. It gets an identity, a start time, a cleanup deadline, and a receipt. The result is a run manifest: a compact record that follows the test from inbox creation to pass or failure. This is a simple idea, but it makes a fake emails generator or temporary inbox tool much more useful. The tool creates the mailbox; the manifest explains what happened around it.

articles.body: A crew annotated image showing where the Artemis II team observed impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. | Image: NASA If you thought you'd seen all there is to see from the Artemis II mission , you're wrong. This week NASA posted over 800GB worth of science data, images, and videos on the Artemis II: Sights & Sounds of Science site. The archive includes over 11,000 photos and videos, over 8.5 hours of audio, and crew-annotated images, such as the one marking where they saw impact flashes on the dark side of the Moon. Together, they offer an unprecedented view inside a historic space mission. One of the more exciting reveals was footage of the Artemis II team telling the ground team back in Houston about its observation of impact flashes.
